### 4.1 Fixed-depth bit-complexity corollary

For each fixed d, the exact compiler restricted to runs with at most d nonempty maximal-block stages has polynomial Turing complexity in the dense rational input size. The polynomial degree may depend on d; this is not a uniform polynomial bound for d up to n.

Use rational nullspace bases and inverses obtained by fraction-free elimination or ratios of minors, not arbitrary long arithmetic circuits. If current coefficients have numerator and denominator bit length at most H, clearing the O(n^4) coefficient denominators costs O(n^4 H) bits. Each relevant minor has size at most n, so its determinant height is polynomial in n and H by the determinant expansion bound. A degree-four linear substitution uses products of at most four basis entries; matrix inversion uses bounded-size determinant ratios; square completion uses quadratic polynomials and one inverse matrix. Directly taking common denominators over the polynomially many coefficients shows that, for absolute constants C,c,

H_next+1 ≤ C(n+1)^c(H+log(n+1)+1).

The same bound covers stored coordinate and curvature matrices. Induction yields H_max ≤ (C(n+1)^c)^d(H_input+log(n+1)+1). Polynomially many integer operations on these heights give a bound (n+1)^(O(d)) times a polynomial in input height, with fixed universal arithmetic exponents. Hence bounded-depth full recovery has a genuine exact bit-complexity guarantee.

# Independent audit: hidden Gaussian quartic compiler

Status: core lemma and successful-certificate reconstruction pass. Full general completeness and polynomial Turing complexity are not established. This audit initially checks the author's equations communicated directly; a final draft check is recorded below when available. No Python was run for this audit.

## 1. Constant-curvature lemma, independently derived

Let V be a real polynomial of degree at most four, globally bounded below. Write V_j for its homogeneous degree-j part and define E={v: D_v V_4=0}. Let C={v: D_v^2 V is constant}.

First V_4 is nonnegative everywhere, by scaling. If v is in C, then D_v^2 V_4=0. Along any affine line parallel to v the polynomial V_4 is affine and globally nonnegative. Its slope must vanish, so D_v V_4=0. Therefore C is contained in E.

Choose any invertible linear coordinates x=A(t,y), with t spanning E. Then V_4 is independent of t. For fixed y, V(A(t,y)) has degree at most three in t and is bounded below. Its homogeneous cubic-in-t term therefore vanishes. Write

V(A(t,y)) = t^T Q(y)t + 2r(y)^T t + s(y).

Q(y) is affine in y, because the quartic part has no t dependence. Boundedness implies Q(y) is positive semidefinite for every y. For each fixed u, u^T Q(y)u is a globally nonnegative affine function of y, hence constant. Polarization shows Q(y)=Q is constant. Thus every v in E has constant second directional derivative, and E=C. Also deg r≤2 and deg s≤4.

If exp(−V) is integrable, Q must be positive definite: any null vector produces, on every fiber y, an exponential of an affine function along that vector, whose integral on the real line diverges whether its slope is zero or not. Tonelli then rules out a finite full integral. This is stronger than mere semidefiniteness and requires integrability, not just boundedness.

Consequently

V(A(t,y))=(t+Q^(−1)r(y))^T Q(t+Q^(−1)r(y))+V_red(y),
V_red=s−r^T Q^(−1)r.

The residual is quartic or lower, bounded below by the same lower bound, and integrable after multiplying by the finite Gaussian fiber integral. The induction hypotheses are preserved.

# Second independent audit: fixed-depth compilation and rounded sampling

Audited source: PROOF.md, SHA256 `4ccf075981c93b856d683a7d38c290341a861315fbae868de6bce3cfc64aff63`.

Date: 4 November 2026. Scope: sections 4.1–4.2, with the earlier algebra inspected for the hypotheses these sections require. Verdict: the stated fixed-depth Turing bound and finite-grid total-variation guarantee are supported. No blocking counterexample was found. This is a mathematical review, not an independently implemented sampler benchmark or novelty clearance.

## 1. Exact input and conditioning

Assume n >= 1, 0 < epsilon < 1, integer p >= 0, dense exact rational coefficients, and a fully successful certificate. A certificate that stops at a nonconstant residual is not covered. Depth d counts nonempty maximal Gaussian blocks; it is fixed for the polynomial-in-original-input claim.

Each stage can be implemented with determinant ratios or fraction-free elimination, followed by direct fixed-degree polynomial substitution. The matrices may have polynomially many rows but at most n columns; relevant nonzero minors have order at most n. Clearing polynomially many denominators and expanding bounded-degree substitutions therefore gives a one-stage height bound polynomial in n times the current coefficient height plus log(n+1). Iterating d times proves n^(O(d)) height growth. It would not prove a uniform polynomial bound for arbitrary d.

A small positive pivot does not create an omitted real-condition-number parameter. A positive rational determinant or LDL pivot of height polynomial in n,H is at least 2^(-poly(n,H)); matrix norms are at most 2^(poly(n,H)). Thus all needed inverse and covariance-factor magnitudes have logarithms polynomial in certificate height. This does not imply practical good conditioning or tolerance to noisy coefficients. It only bounds the bit precision needed for exact rational input.

## 2. Square roots and complete transport evaluation

For Q = L D L^T with positive rational diagonal D, a covariance factor for (2Q)^(-1) is L^(-T) diag((2D_ii)^(-1/2)). Positive rational square roots and reciprocal square roots can be enclosed by rational bisection or integer-root methods. The lower bounds above ensure polynomial bit cost for any prescribed absolute accuracy. There is no hidden exact-real square-root oracle.
